Title: ACT driver licences and vehicle registrations
Summary: Information for ACT residents regarding driver licences and vehicle registrations, and how to transfer them to NSW.
Topics: driver-licence, vehicle-registration, interstate-transfer
Intro: If you live in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT), you’ll need to contact Access Canberra for state/territory government services, including driver licences and vehicle registrations.

Service NSW cannot help you with your ACT licence or rego, unless you’ve moved to NSW and need to:

Note: For Australian Government services, such as Medicare and passports, you’ll need to contact Services Australia.
FAQs:
Q: Where should I contact for ACT driver licences and vehicle registrations?
A: You should contact Access Canberra.
Q: Can Service NSW help me with my ACT driver licence?
A: Service NSW cannot help you with your ACT licence unless you have moved to NSW and need to transfer it to a NSW driver licence.
Q: What if I need to transfer or register my ACT vehicle in NSW?
A: You can use Service NSW to transfer or register your ACT vehicle in NSW.
Eligibility:
- Residents of the Australian Capital Territory (ACT)

Title: Australian passports and visas
Summary: This page provides information on how to apply for or renew Australian passports and visas.
Topics: australian-passports, visas, passport-renewal, travel-documents
Intro: If you need to get a new passport, or renew your old one, you must submit your application through the Australian Passport Office.

All online services are available through the Australian Passport Office website and Australia Post provides a nationwide shopfront if you need to complete part of your application in person.
FAQs:
Q: Where do I apply for a new or renewed Australian passport?
A: You must submit your application through the Australian Passport Office. All online services are available through the Australian Passport Office website.
Q: Can I complete my passport application in person?
A: Australia Post provides a nationwide shopfront if you need to complete part of your application in person.

Title: Bushfire preparation and recovery
Summary: This page provides information and resources to help you prepare for, stay safe during, and recover from a bushfire.
Topics: bushfire-safety, emergency-preparedness, disaster-recovery
FAQs:
Q: How can I stay informed during a bushfire?
A: You can listen to your local ABC radio station, track weather warnings via the Bureau of Emeteorology, and use the Live Traffic NSW app to monitor road closures.
Q: How can I prepare for bushfire season?
A: You can prepare by checking if your home is on bushfire-prone land, checking your access to water, and creating a bushfire survival plan.
Q: What should I do if I am in the event of a bushfire?
A: call the Rural Fire Service (RFS) Bushfire Information Line on 1800 679 737.

Title: Buying a property
Summary: This page provides a guide and information on the process of buying a property in NSW.
Topics: property-buying, home-ownership, grants-and-assistance
FAQs:
Q: Can I use my superannuation to help buy my first home?
A: Yes, through the First Home Super Saver Scheme (FHSS), you can make voluntary contributions to your super and apply to have them released to help you buy your/your first home.
Q: Are there any stamp duty exemptions or concessions for first home buyers?
A: First home buyers may be eligible for exemptions or concessions on transfer (stamp) duty under the First Home Buyers Assistance Scheme.
Q: Can I get a grant for building a new home?
A: If you're a first home buyer who is buying or building a new home, you may qualify for a $10,000 grant under the First Home Owner Grant (New Homes) scheme.

Title: Buying a vehicle
Summary: This guide provides advice and steps for buying a brand new or second-hand vehicle and transferring the registration.
Topics: vehicle-buying, vehicle-registration, vehicle-transfer, car-purchase
FAQs:
Q: How can I find the market value of a vehicle?
A: You can research the vehicle's market value to help negotiate the best price.
Q: What costs should I check before buying a vehicle?
A: Check on-road and operating costs, such as registration, compulsory third party (CTP) insurance, stamp duty, and servicing and spare part costs.
Q: How do I know if a vehicle is allowed for a provisional P1 or P2 driver?
A: You can check prohibited vehicles for provisional P1 and P2 drivers to ensure you are allowed to drive the vehicle.
Q: How can I check if a motor dealer has a valid licence?
A: You can check if the motor dealer has a valid licence through the Service NSW website.
Q: What should I do to transfer a vehicle's registration?
A: The seller must lodge a Notice of Disposal (NOD) and the buyer must transfer the vehicle's registration into their name.

Title: Guide to carer support in NSW
Summary: This guide provides comprehensive information and support contacts for carers in New South Wales.
Topics: carer-support, nsw-health, financial-assistance, disability-support, mental-health
FAQs:
Q: What should I do in a medical emergency?
A: Call Triple Zero (000), or go to a hospital emergency department.
Q: Where can I find support for young carers?
A: Young Carer Hub (call 02 9280 4744) provides counselling, information, and referrals. Carer Gateway (call 1800 422 737) also offers support, advice, and courses.
Q: What financial payments are available to carers?
A: Payments include Carer Payment, Carer Allowance, Carer Supplement, Carer Adjustment Payment, and Child Disability Assistance Payment.
Q: How can I get help with travel concessions?
A: Public transport concessions and subsidies (call 131 500) may be available. Other schemes include the Vision Impaired Person’s Travel Pass and Mobility Parking Scheme (call 13 22 13).
Q: What support is available for mental health carers?
A: Mental Health Carers NSW provides advocacy and support. The NSW Family & Carer Mental Health Program offers training and education for families and carers.
Eligibility:
- Being a carer in NSW
- Caring for a person with a disability or mental illness
- Being a young carer (25 or under)

Title: Change contact details on NSW Government services
Summary: This page provides guides and links to help you change your contact details and personal information across various NSW Government services.
Topics: change-details, nsw-government, contact-details, address-change
FAQs:
Q: How can I change my address with the NSW Government?
A: You can change your address with the NSW Government using this guide.
Q: How do I update my details on a Seniors Card or Savers Card?
A: You can change the details on a NSW Seniors Card or NSW Senior Savers Card using this guide.
Q: Where can I change my contact details for Transport for NSW services?
A: You can change personal details, email, or mobile numbers for various Transport for NSW services.
Eligibility:
- NSW Government service users
- Individuals with various NSW licenses or cards (e.g., Seniors Card, driver licence, boat licence)
- Employees or workers requiring updated registration details (e.g., Working with Children Check, NDIS Worker Check)

Title: Check a business or trade licence
Summary: Use this page to check the licences and registrations for various businesses, tradespeople, and professionals in NSW.
Topics: business-licences, trades, professional-services, nsw-licences
FAQs:
Q: How can I check a business or trade licence?
A: You can check various licences and registrations for businesses, tradespeople, and professionals through specific links on this page.
Q: What types of licences can I check for?
A: You can check licences for areas such as building, construction, design, engineering, liquor, property, and more.
Q: Where can I check a digital trade licence?
A: You can check a digital trade licence or credential using the Service NSW app or the dedicated link.
Eligibility:
- Any citizen or business operating in NSW that needs to verify a licence or registration.

Title: Closing a business
Summary: This guide provides a checklist of tasks and advice needed to properly close down a business.
Topics: closing-a-business, business-obligations, tax-requirements, business-planning
Intro: What you’ll need may depend on:

We’ve gathered a checklist of tasks that commonly need to be completed to close down a business, and included links to useful information and specialist services.
FAQs:
Q: What are the key tasks when closing a business?
A: Key tasks include setting a closing date, ending lease agreements, selling or returning stock, collecting outstanding debts, paying creditors, meeting employee obligations, meeting tax requirements, and cancelling business registrations.
Q: Where can I get professional advice about closing my business?
A: You can seek professional advice from Legal Aid NSW, The Law Society of NSW’s Pro Bono Scheme, Community Legal Centres NSW, The Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman, The Australian Tax Office (ATO), and The Fair Work Ombudsman.
Q: What financial aspects must I review before closing?
A: You must review your finances, including Goods and Services Tax (GST), Capital Gains Tax (CGT), and consider options like liquidation, voluntary administration, receivership, or bankruptcy.
Q: What do I need to do after I close my business?
A: After closing, you must handle sales and purchases, make payments to employees and contractors, pay other businesses, and manage records like receipt books, accounting software, and spreadsheets.

Title: Data breaches
Summary: Provides information and support following data breaches involving companies like Optus and Latitude Financial.
Topics: data-breaches, identity-theft, nsw-driver-licence, document-verification
Intro: The NSW Government is working with both Latitude Financial (March 2023) and Optus (October 2022) to support impacted customers following data breaches of both companies.

More information can be found on the Optus website or the Latitude Financial website.
FAQs:
Q: Who needs a replacement driver licence?
A: You should replace your NSW driver licence, and you will be contacted by the breached company.

Title: Death and bereavement
Summary: This page provides guidance on the steps and services required after a death, covering everything from notifying authorities to arranging a funeral and managing estates.
Topics: death-notification, bereavement, funeral-arrangements, estate-management, death-certificate
FAQs:
Q: What is the first thing I need to do after a death?
A: You must register the death. A death certificate must be issued by the NSW Registry of Births Deaths & Marriages.
Q: Who do I need to notify after a death?
A: You should notify various organisations, including Services Australia (for Centrelink, Medicare, and child support), the Australian Tax Office, and Transport for NSW (for vehicle and vessel licences and registrations).
Q: How do I pay for a funeral?
A: Support is available from several sources, including Services Australia for financial help, the Department of Veterans' Affairs for compensation for ADF members, and understanding who is responsible for payment.
Q: What should I do with my deceased loved one's assets and debts?
A: You need to work out the assets and debt, locate the will, and consider superannuation, which are key parts of managing the estate.
Eligibility:
- Anyone who has experienced a death or is planning for one.

Title: Add a digital licence or credential to the Service NSW app
Summary: Learn how to add various digital licences and credentials, such as your driver licence or trade certificates, to the Service NSW app.
Topics: digital-licences, service-nsw-app, credentials, licences
FAQs:
Q: How do I add a licence or credential to the Service NSW app?
A: Download the Service NSW app, log in with your MyServiceNSW Account details, select 'Wallet' from the homescreen, and then tap the 'Add' button to follow the prompts.
Q: Do I need to carry a physical card for all my licences?
A: You must carry your physical card when operating a personal watercraft at any speed, and when you are working with a trade licence, certificate, or training card.
Q: What licences can I add to the Service NSW app?
A: You can add licences and credentials such as the NSW Digital Driver Licence, Boat driving licence, Recreational fishing licence, RSA/RCG Competency Card, Seniors Card/Senior Savers Card, and trade licences/certificates.
Eligibility:
- Must have a MyServiceNSW Account to log in to the Service NSW app.
- For the RSA/RCG Competency Card, your email address must be the same for both the card and your MyServiceNSW Account.

Title: Guide to help people impacted by domestic and family violence
Summary: This guide provides information and resources for people impacted by domestic and family violence, including emergency contacts and safety advice.
Topics: domestic-and-family-violence, safety, emergency-services, online-safety
Intro: Domestic and family violence can include, but is not limited to:

If you, or someone you know, is impacted by domestic and family violence, the following transactions and services may assist in establishing and maintaining safety.

If you need to access a safer computer, consider using one at work, at school, at a library, or at a Service NSW service centre.
FAQs:
Q: What should I do if I am in immediate danger?
A: Call Emergency Triple Zero (000) if you or your children are in immediate danger.
Q: Where can I get free counselling and referral services?
A: The NSW Domestic Violence Line offers free counselling and referral services, available 24 hours, 7 days a week. Call 1800 656 463.
Q: What resources are available for safety planning?
A: You can visit the 'make a safety plan' resource for help with safety planning.

Title: Drought support
Summary: Find support services and resources for managing the impacts of drought in NSW.
Topics: drought, support, agriculture, financial-help
FAQs:
Q: Where can I get help with savings?
A: You can get help from a Savings Finder specialist at a regional Service NSW Centre or on board the Mobile Service Centres.
Q: What support is available for farming and soil health?
A: Support services include Drought Adoption Officers and resources for saving soils during drought.
Q: Where can I find more information about drought support?
A: You can visit the NSW DroughtHub for comprehensive information.

Title: Guide to eyesight testing for NSW driver and rider licences
Summary: This guide explains the requirements and procedures for eyesight testing for NSW driver and rider licences.
Topics: eyesight-test, driver-licence, rider-licence, nsw-licence
FAQs:
Q: When do I need to pass an eyesight test?
A: You must pass an eyesight test when applying for a driver or rider licence for the first time, when upgrading a licence to a higher class, or at specific intervals based on your age and circumstances.
Q: How often do I need eyesight tests based on my age?
A: The frequency varies: every 10 years if under 45, every 5 years if over 45, and every year from age 75. You also need one if you haven't passed a test in the 12 months before renewing or replacing a licence, or when applying for a 10-year licence.
Q: What happens if I have vision issues or need special conditions on my licence?
A: The guide covers conditions such as vision in one eye only (monocular vision), Glaucoma, and Macular degeneration, and details specific licence conditions (S001, S002, S003) that may apply.
Eligibility:
- Individuals applying for a driver or rider licence for the first time
- Individuals upgrading a licence to a higher class
- Drivers and riders renewing or replacing a licence
- Drivers and riders who are 45 years or older
- Drivers and riders who are 75 years or older
- Drivers and riders who have specific medical conditions or roles (e.g., heavy vehicle drivers, passenger transport service drivers)

Summary: This guide provides information on where to look and who to contact if you have found lost or unclaimed money.

FAQs:

A: You can check for unpaid wages through the relevant service.

Q: Where can I find forms related to birth, death, and marriage?
A: Forms for births, deaths, and marriages include certificates, corrections, and letters of authority.

Summary: Find free tools and support to help your small business manage debt and plan its next steps if it is under financial pressure.

Title: Get a NSW driver licence guide
Summary: This guide outlines the steps and requirements for obtaining different types of NSW driver and provisional licences.
Topics: driver-licence, provisional-licence, heavy-vehicle-licence, road-rules
FAQs:
Q: What are the steps to get a NSW driver licence?
A: The process involves being 16 or older, passing the Driver Knowledge Test (DKT), reading the Road User Handbook, taking practice tests, and then following steps for the learner, P1, P2, and full licences.
Q: How do I get a provisional P1 licence?
A: To get a P1 licence, you must complete the required driving hours and record your time in a learner driver log book.
Q: What are the requirements for a full licence?
A: To get a full licence, you must prove your identity, pass an eyesight test, and pay the licence fee.
Q: Can I transfer an interstate or overseas licence?
A: Yes, the page provides specific processes for transferring probationary interstate, interstate, and overseas driver licences.
Eligibility:
- Be 16 years of age or older.
- Pass the Driver Knowledge Test (DKT).
- Complete required driving hours and record time in a learner driver log book to be eligible for a P1 licence.
- Pass the Hazard Perception Test (HPT) and the driving test to get a P1 licence.
- Pass the driving test and prove identity and pay the licence fee to get a full licence.

Title: Getting married
Summary: This page provides information on the processes for getting married, registering relationships, and changing names in NSW.
Topics: getting-married, relationships, name-changes
FAQs:
Q: How do I start the process of getting married?
A: You must first apply for a Notice of Intended Marriage. You can apply online using the Notice of Intended Marriage application link.
Q: Where can I get married?
A: You can apply to get married at a Registry Office.
Q: What if I am divorced and need to prove it?
A: You can request a proof of divorce order.
Q: How do I register a relationship in NSW?
A: You can apply to register a relationship in NSW. If you need to withdraw this application, you can use the withdrawal link.
Eligibility:
- Must apply for a Notice of Intended Marriage before getting married.
- Must apply to get married at a Registry Office.

Title: Going to local or small claims court
Summary: This guide provides information on appealing fines, licences, or registration issues by going to a local or small claims court.
Topics: local-court, small-claims-court, fines, legal-support, court-process
Intro: If you are thinking about appealing a fine, licence or registration issue, this guide links to information about:
FAQs:
Q: What should I do if I want to appeal a fine?
A: You can pay the fine, or you can find more information about going to court for a fine. Legal Aid NSW also has an online tool to help you work out the best way to deal with your legal problem.
Q: Where can I get legal help and support?
A: You can contact an organization that offers legal help and support. Special court support services are available for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and you can get help with translation or disability support.
Q: How can I represent myself in court?
A: Representing yourself in court gives you access to your case information, allows you to file documents, and manages your profile in the NSW Courts and Tribunals services.
Q: What do I need to know about the court process?
A: Information is available on what to wear, the people you will see, and how to behave inside a courtroom (Attending the Local Court). You can also learn about the court journey, and what to know about charges, bail, and appearing in court (Going to court as a defendant).
Eligibility:
- Individuals appealing a fine, licence, or registration issue.

Summary: This guide explains how to update your address and personal details across various NSW government services, including licences, registrations, and records.

Q: Do I need to know anything before using these calculators?

Summary: This page provides information and links for parents on various aspects of having a baby, including financial support, registering the birth, and obtaining certificates.

Q: How do I register a baby's birth?

Title: How to upload documents for an online application
Summary: This page explains how to prepare and upload documents when applying for a NSW Government service online.
Topics: online-application, uploading-documents, document-format, digital-documents, scanned-documents
Intro: When you apply for a NSW Government service or support, you might need to provide details from a document to confirm your identity or prove your eligibility. Sometimes we'll ask you to upload a copy of the document to confirm your details.

Make sure your name, address and all the details requested are clearly visible when you submit your documents.
FAQs:
Q: What details must be visible when I submit my documents?
A: Ensure that your name, address, and all requested details are clearly visible on the documents you submit.
Q: What are the requirements for the file name and format?
A: The file must be saved in the requested format (such as JPEG, JPG, PDF, PNG, or TIF), be less than 6 MB, and include only letters and numbers in the file name (no spaces or special characters).
Q: How should I handle digital documents?
A: If you have digital documents, ask the provider to email you a copy, save the attachments to your device, and then upload them when you apply online.
Q: How do I upload documents if I only have photos?
A: If you take a photo of documents, email the photo to yourself, open the email on a computer or tablet, and save the image as a JPEG, JPG, PDF, PNG, or TIF file before uploading.

Q: What levels of government are represented in Australia?
A: Australia has three elected levels of government: federal, state/territory, and local.
Q: How can I find my local or state electorate?
A: You can find your state district, council, and ward electorate using the NSW Electoral Commission website.
Q: What are the different ways I can vote?

Title: Losing your driver licence (suspension)
Summary: This page provides information on why a driver licence might be suspended and what steps to take regarding the suspension and appeal process.
Topics: driver-licence, suspension, demerit-points, traffic-offences
FAQs:
Q: Why might my driver licence be suspended?
A: Suspension can occur for several reasons, including exceeding your demerit points limit, not paying outstanding fines, medical reasons, or committing a traffic offence (such as car, rider, or heavy vehicle offences).
Q: What happens if I receive an on-the-spot suspension from the police?
A: If the suspension is on the spot, it begins immediately, and you cannot drive away; someone else must pick up your vehicle. If it happens within 48 hours of being charged, the suspension may be automatic (3 or 6 months) or remain in place until your case is heard by a court.
Q: How do I appeal a licence suspension?
A: You must file your appeal within 28 days of the date you were suspended. You can find specific guidance on appealing the suspension or cancellation for medical reasons, or generally appealing the suspension.
Q: When can I drive again after a suspension?
A: You may be able to drive again if you buy a driving record online, call 13 77 88, visit a Service NSW Centre, successfully appeal the suspension, or are found not guilty in court.
Eligibility:
- Individuals who have lost or had their driver licence suspended.
- Individuals who need to understand the reasons for licence suspension (e.g., demerit points, unpaid fines, medical issues, traffic offences).

Title: Medicare in Australia
Summary: This page provides general information about Medicare in Australia, including who is eligible and what services are covered.
Topics: medicare, health-care, australia, enrolling
Intro: Service NSW does not provide any Medicare-related services.
FAQs:
Q: Who is eligible for Medicare?
A: Australians and certain overseas visitors are eligible for free or subsidised health services through Medicare.
Q: What services are covered by Medicare?
A: Medicare covers free or subsidised treatment by health professionals (like doctors and specialists), free treatment in public hospitals, and 75% of the Medicare schedule fee for private patients in public or private hospitals.
Q: How do I claim a Medicare benefit?
A: You need a doctor's invoice for the service and proof of payment if you paid for the services in full.
Q: How can I replace a lost or damaged Medicare card?
A: You can request a new card via your myGov account linked to Medicare, call Medicare general enquiries on 132 011, or visit a Medicare Service Centre with your proof of identity.
Eligibility:
- Australians
- Certain overseas visitors

Title: Mental wellbeing resources
Summary: This page provides a comprehensive list of resources, services, and support options for mental wellbeing.
Topics: mental-health, support, wellbeing, crisis-support
FAQs:
Q: What are the 24/7 telephone services available for mental health support?
A: You can call the NSW Mental Health Line on 1800 011 511, Lifeline Australia on 13 11 14, Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Mensline Australia on 1300 789 978, Kids Helpline on 1800 551 800 (for children and young people aged 5 to 25), Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467, or 13YARN on 13 92 76.
Q: Where can I access face-to-face mental health services?
A: Face-to-face services include your local General Practitioner (GP), the National Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (NACCHO), Mobile Service Centres, and Headspace Centre (for young people aged 12 to 25).
Q: What support is available after a natural disaster?

Topics: fines, payment-plan, overdue-fine, revenue-nsw
Intro: If you cannot pay your fine or overdue fine in full by the due date, you can pay over a longer period by setting up a payment plan.

A payment plan allows you to break down your payment into smaller amounts that are made via instalments. When you set up a payment plan, you pay an agreed sum of money weekly or fortnightly until the balance is cleared.

You may be eligible to repay your fines by doing unpaid work, courses, counselling, mentoring or treatment programs, through a Work and Development Order. Call 1300 478 879 before your fine's due date for more information.
FAQs:
Q: How can I pay my fine in smaller amounts?
A: You can set up a payment plan to break down your payment into smaller amounts made via instalments, paid weekly or fortnightly.
Q: What if I cannot pay my fine by the due date?
A: You can set up a payment plan if you cannot pay your fine or overdue fine in full by the due date.
Q: Can I repay my fines through unpaid work?
A: You may be eligible to repay your fines by doing unpaid work, courses, counselling, mentoring, or treatment programs through a Work and Development Order. Call 1300 478 879 before your fine's due date for more information.
Eligibility:
- Cannot pay the fine or overdue fine in full by the due date.

Title: Apply for a provisional P1 driver licence
Summary: You can apply for a provisional P1 driver licence if you meet the required criteria and pass the necessary tests.
Topics: driver-licence, provisional-p1, nsw-licence, driving-test
Intro: You can apply for a provisional P1 driver licence if you've held a NSW learner licence for the required period of time, and passed the necessary tests. You can also apply if you've passed the driving test as a holder of an interstate learner licence, provisional licence or an overseas licence.

Applications for the licence are made at a service centre, and if you wish you can apply for a NSW Photo Card at the same time, and take advantage of paying a reduced application fee for it.
FAQs:
Q: Who can apply for a P1 driver licence?
A: You can apply if you are at least 17 years of age and have held a learner licence for the required period, or if you passed the driving test using an interstate, provisional, or overseas licence.
Q: What do I need to apply for a P1 licence?
A: You need the 'Licence Application' PDF form, your current learner licence, proof of identity documents, and your payment.
Q: Do I need to take a special assessment if I have a disability?
A: If you live with a disability, talk to your doctor about a possible Occupational Therapist driving assessment before applying. You may be eligible for a Disability driving test.
Eligibility:
- Be at least 17 years of age.
- Have held a learner licence for at least 12 months (if aged between 17 and 24).
- Have logged the required driving hours.
- Have passed the Hazard Perception Test (HPT).

Title: Apply for a Working with Children Check
Summary: Find out about and apply for a Working with Children Check (WWCC), which is required for working or volunteering with children in NSW.
Topics: working-with-children-check, nsw, child-safety, police-check
Intro: The Working with Children Check (WWCC) is a requirement for anyone who works or volunteers in child-related work in NSW. It involves a National Police Check (criminal history record check) and a review of reportable workplace misconduct.

Results of a National Police Check can take up to 4 weeks to be received.

The outcome of a check is either a clearance to work with children or a bar against working with children. If cleared, the check will be valid for 5 years, however applicants are continuously monitored.

The application costs $107 for paid workers and is free for volunteers.
FAQs:
Q: How long is a Working with Children Check valid for?
A: If cleared, the check will be valid for 5 years, although applicants are continuously monitored.
Q: How much does the Working with Children Check cost?
A: The application costs $107 for paid workers and is free for volunteers.
Q: What is required to apply for a Working with Children Check?
A: You must be aged 18 or over.
Eligibility:
- Must be aged 18 or over.

Q: How much is the Seniors Energy Rebate?
A: Eligible customers receive $200 each financial year.
Q: What documents do I need to apply?
A: You need a MyServiceNSW Account, your Commonwealth Seniors Health Card with your Customer Reference Number (CRN) or Department of Veterans' Affairs file number, your most recent electricity bill (issued on or after 1 July in the 2025–26 financial year), and your bank account details.

Title: Apply to go to court for a fine
Summary: You can apply to have a fine matter heard and decided in court if you received a fine notice, reminder notice, or overdue fine.
Topics: fines, court, penalty, overdue-fine
Intro: If you received a fine (fine notice, fine reminder notice or overdue fine), you can apply to have the matter heard and decided in court.

### When to apply

You need to apply before the due date on your fine reminder notice.

If you paid your fine before the overdue date, you have 90 days from the date the fine was issued to go to court.

If your fine is overdue, see Apply to go to court for an overdue fine.

### Other options

Before applying to go to court you should consider:

If you're having difficulty paying your fine, you can:

FAQs:
Q: When do I need to apply to go to court?
A: You must apply before the due date on your fine reminder notice. If you paid your fine before the overdue date, you have 90 days from the date the fine was issued to go to court.
Q: Who can apply to have the fine matter heard in court?
A: The person named on the fine notice, the vehicle owner (if no name is on the notice), or the authorised representative of the person named on the notice (who must complete the Authority to Act form).
Q: What do I need to apply to go to court?
A: You need your name, date of birth, driver licence details, residential address (PO boxes are not accepted) for the Court Attendance Notice (CAN), your fine notice number, and the date of the offence.

Title: Nominate someone else for a fine
Summary: You can transfer a fine by nominating the person who was actually responsible for the offence.
Topics: fines, nominate-driver, offence-details, transport-nsw
Intro: If you receive a fine (fine notice, fine reminder notice or overdue fine) but were not the driver or person responsible for the offence, you can transfer the fine by nominating the person responsible.

Some offences, such as camera-detected offences and parking in a school zone, will apply demerit points to a driver licence, so you are required by law to nominate the person responsible. For offences such as littering from a vehicle, you should name the person responsible, even if you were the driver at the time.

If the fine is under a company name, then an authorised person from your company must nominate the driver or person responsible.
FAQs:
Q: Do I have to nominate the person responsible for the fine?
A: Yes, you are required by law to nominate the person responsible for offences such as camera-detected offences and parking in a school zone. You should also name the person responsible for offences like littering from a vehicle, even if you were the driver.
Q: What if the fine is under a company name?
A: An authorised person from your company must nominate the driver or person responsible.
Q: How do I nominate someone else for a fine?
A: Select the 'Go to myPenalty' button and follow the prompts to name the driver or person responsible.
Eligibility:
- Received a fine (fine notice, fine reminder notice, or overdue fine) but were not the driver or person responsible for the offence.

Title: Complete a Notice of Intended Marriage form
Summary: This page provides information on completing the legal Notice of Intended Marriage form before getting married in Australia.
Topics: marriage, notice-of-intended-marriage, wedding-requirements, celebrant
Intro: Before you get married, you must complete a Notice of Intended Marriage. The form is a legal requirement for getting married in Australia.

Part of the form needs to be completed by you and the other part by your authorised marriage celebrant.

You need to give the form and your identity documents to your marriage celebrant at least one month before the wedding date.
FAQs:
Q: Do I need to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident to get married?
A: No, you do not have to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident to get married in Australia.
Q: How far in advance do I need to give the form to my celebrant?
A: You need to give the form and your identity documents to your marriage celebrant at least one month before the wedding date.
Q: Who can witness the signing of the form?
A: An authorised person needs to witness your signature and sign the form. If you are outside Australia, see the form for a list of authorised witnesses you can use.
Eligibility:
- Be aged 18 years or older, unless a court has approved a marriage where one person is 16 to 18 years old.
- Not already be married.
- You do not have to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident to get married in Australia.

Title: Register a birth
Summary: This page provides information on how and when to register a baby's birth in NSW.
Topics: register-a-birth, new-baby, nsw-birth-registration, birth-certificate
Intro: You should register your baby within 60 days of the birth.

After 60 days, you can still register a birth but you may be asked for additional details. The registration can also take longer to process.

Parents have 180 days to register their baby’s birth if their child is born with variations of sex characteristics that do not allow for an easy assignment of sex.

It's free to register a birth. There is a fee if you want to order a birth certificate.
FAQs:
Q: How long do I have to register a baby's birth?
A: You should register your baby within 60 days of the birth. If the baby is born with variations of sex characteristics that do not allow for an easy assignment of sex, parents have 180 days to register the birth.
Q: Is it free to register a birth?
A: Registering a birth is free. There is a fee only if you want to order a birth certificate.
Q: What do I need to register a birth online?
A: You will need identity documents for each parent listed on the birth registration. For online registration, you can enter licence and card numbers instead of uploading copies.
Eligibility:
- You are the parent of the baby and the baby was born in NSW.
- Other people such as grandparents and case workers can register a birth using the paper form application method.
- If the baby was born in Wodonga and the parent lives in Albury, the registration can be done in either NSW or Victoria, but not both.

Title: Register a change of name
Summary: You can register a change of name online, but you must check eligibility and requirements first.
Topics: change-of-name, nsw-registry, identity-documents, name-change-rules
Intro: If you want to change your name, you can do it online. You can change your name only once in a 12-month period and 3 times in your lifetime.

Changing your name or the name of a child is a complex process. For information on eligibility, required documents and how to apply, visit Change of name – NSW Registry of Births, Deaths & Marriages.
FAQs:
Q: How many times can I change my name?
A: You can change your name up to 3 times in your lifetime, and you can only change it once within a 12-month period.
Q: Can parents change a child's name?
A: Yes, parents, guardians, and caseworkers can register a change of name for children under 18 years.
Q: Where can I find information on eligibility and required documents?
A: You must check the eligibility and document requirements at Change of name – NSW Registry of Births, Deaths & Marriages.
Eligibility:
- Were born or adopted in NSW.
- Were born overseas and have lived in NSW for the past 3 years.
- Have not changed your name with any Australian Registry in the past 12 months.
- Have not previously registered 3 official changes of name in Australia.
- Parents, guardians, and caseworkers can register a change of name for children under 18 years.

Q: How do I pay for my vehicle registration renewal online?

Q: Who is eligible to renew a vehicle registration online?

Title: Renew or upgrade a NSW driver licence
Summary: You can renew or upgrade your NSW Driver Licence online if you meet specific eligibility criteria.
Topics: driver-licence, renew, upgrade, nsw
Intro: If you meet certain eligibility criteria, you can renew or upgrade your NSW Driver Licence online.

The term that you renew or upgrade for depends on the licence class:

Note: You'll need to visit a Service NSW Centre in person if you'd like a 10-year licence (available for drivers aged 21 to 44) or if any of the reasons you may not be able to renew or upgrade online apply to you.
FAQs:
Q: Do I need to visit a Service NSW Centre in person?
A: You must visit a Service NSW Centre in person if you want a 10-year licence (for drivers aged 21 to 44) or if any of the reasons listed prevent you from renewing or upgrading online.
Q: What are the eyesight requirements for renewal?
A: If you are less than 45 years old, you must have passed an eyesight test within 10.5 years of the new licence expiring. If you are 45 years or older, you must have passed an eyesight test within 5.5 years of the new licence expiring.
Q: What happens if I have a dual class licence?
A: If you are 25 years or over and hold a dual class licence where one class is full C, LR, MR, HR, HC, or MC, and the other class is R P1 (held for at least 12 months) or R P2, the provisional class will automatically upgrade to full when you renew the full class.
Eligibility:
- You must meet the eyesight requirements.
- You must hold an eligible driver licence that expires in 6 months or less, or one that expired no more than 6 months ago.
- You must be aged 17 years or over (up to 70 if your licence class is MC).
- Your up-to-date medical conditions must be recorded with Transport for NSW (TfNSW), and your NSW Fitness to Drive medical assessment must not be overdue.
- Your licence must not be subject to any restrictions related to enforcement (e.g., cancelled, disqualified, suspended, refused, or pending an appeal or suspension decision).
- You must have had your signature and photograph taken by TfNSW within 10.5 years before the new licence expires.

Title: Replace a NSW Driver Licence
Summary: Learn how to replace a lost, stolen, destroyed, or expired NSW driver licence, and find out if you can do it online or if you need to visit a Service NSW Centre.
Topics: driver-licence, nsw, replace, service-nsw
Intro: In certain instances, you may find it necessary to replace your driver licence. For example, it could have been lost, stolen, destroyed, or involved in a data breach.

If you meet the eligibility criteria, you can order a replacement online.

If you do not meet the eligibility criteria, or you'd like to apply for a NSW Photo Card at the same time, you'll need to visit a Service NSW Centre.

When you replace your licence, your driver licence number remains the same but your card number changes. This protects you from unauthorised Document Verification Service checks using the old card's information.
FAQs:
Q: What happens to my driver licence number when I replace it?
A: Your driver licence number remains the same, but your card number changes. This helps protect you from unauthorised Document Verification Service checks using the old card's information.
Q: Who is eligible to replace their licence online?
A: You may be eligible if you changed your address within the last 14 days, ordered a replacement online in the last 12 months, want to apply for a NSW Photo Card at the same time, or if your licence has been disqualified, cancelled, suspended, or expired.
Q: What do I need to replace my licence?
A: You need a MyServiceNSW Account and the licence fee or your concession card details.
Eligibility:
- You changed your address within the last 14 days.
- You ordered a replacement licence online in the last 12 months.
- You want to apply for a NSW Photo Card at the same time.
- You've been prohibited from driving a motor vehicle or riding a motorcycle in NSW or elsewhere since last obtaining your licence.
- Your licence has been disqualified, cancelled, suspended, or expired.
- You are not eligible to order a replacement online and will need to visit a service centre if any of the following apply.

Q: What documents are needed if I am transferring to the executor or administrator?
A: You must provide the original or certified copy of the will, probate, or letters of administration. If these are unavailable, you need signed, written advice from a solicitor or NSW Trustee & Guardian.

Title: Transfer an interstate driver licence
Summary: Learn how to transfer your interstate driver licence to a NSW licence after moving to the state.
Topics: driver-licence, interstate, nsw, transfer
Intro: If you've moved to NSW from another Australian state or territory, you can only drive in NSW on an interstate licence for 3 months. After that period you'll need to visit a Service NSW Centre and apply to transfer your licence to a NSW driver licence.

Sometimes interstate checks need to be made so allow plenty of time for a transfer to be processed.

There's no fee to transfer a current unrestricted or provisional licence. If your licence has expired, or is just about to, a fee will be charged.

Note that drivers 75 years or older are required to undergo a medical review, and may have to take a practical driving test.
FAQs:
Q: How long can I drive in NSW on an interstate licence?
A: You can only drive in NSW on an interstate licence for 3 months. After that period, you must apply to transfer your licence to a NSW driver licence.
Q: Is there a fee to transfer my licence?
A: There is no fee to transfer a current unrestricted or provisional licence. However, a fee will be charged if your licence has expired, or is about to.
Q: Do I need to take a medical review?
A: Drivers 75 years or older are required to undergo a medical review and may have to take a practical driving test.
Eligibility:
- You must have moved to NSW from another Australian state or territory.

Title: Transfer an overseas driver licence
Summary: Learn how to transfer an overseas driver licence to a NSW licence.
Topics: driver-licence, overseas-licence, nsw
Intro: If you're an Australian citizen or permanent resident, or if you hold a New Zealand driver licence, you can drive in NSW on an overseas licence for 3 months. Within this 3-month period however, you'll need to visit a Service NSW Centre and transfer your overseas licence to a NSW Driver Licence.

You may need to pass a knowledge or driving test, depending on where your overseas licence was issued. View a list of Recognised countries and jurisdictions.

Drivers 75 years or older are required to undergo a medical review and may need to take a practical driving test.

If you're a temporary visa holder or you cannot provide proof of permanent residency, you can apply for a NSW licence as a temporary overseas visitor.

Note: Holders of licences from certain countries may be required to obtain a validation letter from the relevant consulate or licensing authority. For information regarding validation requirements, please call 13 77 88 or visit a service centre.
FAQs:
Q: How long can I drive in NSW on an overseas licence?
A: If you are an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or hold a New Zealand licence, you can drive in NSW on an overseas licence for 3 months.
Q: What do I need to do to transfer my licence?
A: You must visit a Service NSW Centre to transfer your overseas licence to a NSW Driver Licence. You may need to pass a knowledge or driving test.
Q: Are there special requirements for older drivers?
A: Drivers 75 years or older are required to undergo a medical review and may need to take a practical driving test.
Eligibility:
- Australian citizen or permanent resident
- New Zealand licence holder
- Temporary overseas visitor (if unable to provide proof of permanent residency)
